newsitem.title: USA: U.S. productivity growth moderate at end of 1996.
newsitem.headline: U.S. productivity growth moderate at end of 1996.

text.p: The productivity of American workers grew moderately at the end of 1996, the government said on Tuesday in revised figures that presented a less upbeat picture of the economy than previous indicated.
The Labour Department reported that outside of the agricultural sector, productivity, or output per worker hour, rose at an annual rate of 1.1 percent in the fourth quarter.
The rate was consistent with the long-run average for productivity and was a sharp improvement from the third quarter, when productivity was flat.
However, the fourth-quarter number was far less impressive than the 2.2 percent jump the department had originally estimated for the final 1996 quarter.
It was also more modest than the 1.5 increase projected by Wall Street economists.
The productivity gain for all of 1996 was also revised downward, to 0.7 percent from the previously reported 0.8 percent.
Amid rapid economic growth recently, gains in productivity, which allow businesses to increase their output without raising their costs, are seen as crucial to containing inflation.
Financial markets, increasingly concerned that the Federal Reserve might raise interest rates to try to head off inflation, have been watching productivity figures closely.
The fourth-quarter productivity jump came as output overall in the non-farm sector surged 5.0 percent, while hours worked rose 3.9 percent and real hourly compensation edged up 0.2 percent.
That helped to keep the rise in unit-labour costs fairly small at 2.5 percent, although the newly reported increase in costs was higher than the previous estimate of 1.4 percent.
